claims.text: The quaternary equiatomic alloy has an FCC structure, high configurational entropy, significant atomic-size mismatch, and high lattice distortion.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate above a critical strain rate of approximately 10^-2 s^-1.
The loss of strain-rate sensitivity is caused by saturation of thermally activated dislocation glide.
Above the critical strain rate, the dominant deformation mechanism shifts from dislocation glide to localized shear banding.
Localized shear banding is driven by severe lattice friction rather than a deformation-induced phase transformation.
High-density forest dislocations interact with solute-induced lattice-distortion fields that create a high Peierls barrier.
At low strain rates, dislocations move by thermal activation over local energy barriers created by solute atoms.
Increasing strain rate makes the available thermal-activation time insufficient for dislocations to overcome local barriers.
As strain rate increases, the stress required for dislocation motion approaches an athermal limit identified with the Peierls stress.
After the athermal limit is reached, further increases in strain rate do not significantly increase yield strength.
A stress-induced phase transformation would exhibit a strain-rate dependence or hysteresis distinct from dislocation saturation.
Yield strength plotted against logarithmic strain rate will increase linearly at low rates and reach a zero-slope plateau at high rates.
Post-deformation microscopy will show high dislocation densities and slip bands.
Post-deformation characterization will show no deformation-induced HCP or BCC phase.
In solid-solution-strengthened FCC alloys, yield strength typically follows a power-law or logarithmic strain-rate dependence until an athermal limit is reached.
The proposed behavior applies when thermal activation is significant at low strain rates but insufficient at high strain rates.
A stress-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation would produce nonlinear strain-rate dependence and microstructural changes not explained by dislocation saturation.
The critical strain rate depends strongly on elemental composition and the magnitude of lattice distortion.
Extremely low stacking-fault energy could allow deformation twinning to compete with or dominate dislocation glide and alter strain-rate sensitivity.
New non-FCC diffraction peaks during deformation, or continued linear strengthening beyond the proposed threshold without evidence of dislocation saturation, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The plateau is predicted to begin at approximately 10^-2 s^-1, but the experiment labels 10^-3 s^-1 as a rate where the plateau is predicted.

The hypothesis states that the dominant mechanism shifts from dislocation glide to localized shear banding, whereas the mechanism field explains the plateau solely through dislocation motion approaching an athermal limit and does not explain the onset or rate control of shear banding.

The predicted outcome associates absence of new HCP or BCC phases with absence of deformation twinning, while the uncertainty field treats twinning as a possible competing mechanism. Twinning can occur within FCC material without creating a new crystallographic phase, so the proposed phase test does not consistently distinguish twinning from glide.
